opus-5.5.text:
That's a good question, and honestly my view has changed quite a lot.

Early in my career, especially as a PhD student and in my first years as a researcher, I cared a lot about those external signals. How many papers did I get into CVPR or NeurIPS? Did we get an oral? Was there a best paper nomination? Part of that is natural. When you're young, you don't yet have a clear sense of your own taste, so you lean on other people's judgment to tell you whether you're doing good work. Those signals also matter practically, for getting a job, for getting people to take you seriously.

Over time, though, I've come to think they are a fairly noisy proxy for what really matters. A best paper award reflects what a small committee found exciting at one moment. Some award-winning papers are quickly forgotten, and some papers that were rejected once or twice end up shaping a whole direction. I've seen that happen many times, including with work I was involved in.

So now the question I ask myself is much simpler: did this work change what people can do? Do other researchers build on it? Do engineers actually use it? Did it move the field toward something we care about, like systems that can understand and simulate the physical world? That kind of impact takes years to show up. It doesn't fit neatly into a conference cycle.

I'd also say that once you lead a team, your perspective shifts. It's less about my own record and more about whether the people I work with are growing and whether we, as a group, are tackling problems that are big enough. Chasing paper counts can push you toward safe, incremental work, and that's the opposite of what I want for the team.

That said, I don't want to sound dismissive. Recognition still feels nice, and it's encouraging for students and junior researchers, so I'm happy when they get it. But I now treat it as a pleasant side effect, not the goal. The goal is to work on something you believe is important, do it really well, and let time be the judge.

r001.rationale: The candidate says his focus shifted from his own paper record to whether the people he works with are growing, describing a move toward helping others.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it has changed a lot. When I was a PhD student and then in my early years as a researcher, those external measures mattered enormously to me. Getting a paper into CVPR or NeurIPS, getting an oral, getting a best paper nomination, these felt like the scoreboard. You are young, you don't have a track record yet, and the community gives you very few signals about whether you are doing well. So awards and acceptance counts become the proxy. I remember being quite anxious around review season, refreshing the page, feeling that my value as a researcher went up or down depending on the decision.

Over time, that faded, for a few reasons. One is simply that once you have been through many cycles, you see how noisy the process is. I have had papers rejected that later became some of my most cited and most used work, and I have had papers accepted that nobody remembers. When you observe that enough times, it is hard to keep treating acceptance as ground truth about quality.

The second reason is that my job changed. At NVIDIA, leading a research team, the question is no longer "did this paper win something," but "did this work actually change what people can do." With generative models in particular, the feedback loop is very concrete. Did artists use it? Did it ship into a product? Did another group build on top of it? Those signals are slower and messier than an award, but they are much more honest.

And the third reason is more personal. At some point you realize that chasing recognition pushes you toward safe, incremental problems, because those are the ones that reliably get accepted. The problems I actually care about now are the ones where you might work for two or three years and have nothing to show at a conference. If I let the award count drive me, I would never work on those.

So I would say the importance has gone from being central to being almost a byproduct. I still appreciate recognition, I am not pretending to be above it, and for the students and junior researchers on my team, I know it matters for their careers, so I take it seriously on their behalf. But for myself, the measure I pay attention to now is whether the work is still standing five years later.

r001.rationale: The response clearly says accolades became less central and emphasizes whether research changes what people can do or gets used. It does not clearly describe Ming-Yu Liu’s own priority as shifting toward helping other people.

astra-6.text:
Earlier in my career, I cared a lot about those things. A best paper award or recognition from the community felt like confirmation that I was doing good research. I think that’s natural when you’re starting out and trying to establish yourself.

Over time, I’ve put less weight on those external measures. I still appreciate recognition, but I’m more interested in whether the work actually matters. Does it solve a meaningful problem? Does it enable someone to do something they couldn’t do before? Is it something I’m proud of, even if it doesn’t win an award?

So I wouldn’t say those measures have become irrelevant. They’re just no longer the main thing guiding what I choose to work on.

r001.rationale: The candidate says external recognition matters less and emphasizes work that “enable[s] someone to do something they couldn’t do before,” describing a shift toward benefiting others.

sol-6.1.text:
Earlier in my career, I paid more attention to those things. When you’re starting out, you want some indication that you’re doing good research, and papers and awards give you a concrete signal. They also help you establish yourself.

Over time, I’ve become more interested in whether the work actually matters. Did we solve a meaningful problem? Are people using what we developed? Did it open up something that wasn’t possible before? Those questions are harder to measure, but I find them more motivating now.

It’s still nice to receive recognition. But I wouldn’t want to choose a research direction just because I thought it might win an award. I’d rather work on something I believe in and let the recognition follow, if it does.

r001.rationale: The response shifts from awards and papers toward meaningful problems, use, and what the work enables. It does not clearly say that helping other people is the new priority.
